prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
# 10 Stocks to Buy on January 2, 2019

**A caveat first:** I know how 2019–2023 actually turned out, and I can't fully set that aside, so this list can't be a clean forecast. I've tried to use only reasoning that was mainstream and defensible on that date, but treat it as a thought exercise, not a real test of stock-picking skill.

## The setup (January 2, 2019)

- The S&P 500 just finished 2018 down about 6%, after a roughly 20% drop in Q4.
- The main worries are Fed rate hikes, the US–China tariff war, a flattening yield curve and fears of a 2019 recession.
- Many high-quality growth companies are 20–50% below their 2018 highs.

The strategy is to buy dominant, cash-generating franchises with long growth runways while they're on sale. A small defensive position helps in case the recession arrives.

## The 10 picks

| # | Company | Why buy now | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Microsoft (MSFT)** | Azure is growing about 75% a year. Office 365 is turning the installed base into recurring revenue. Under Nadella, execution is strong and the balance sheet is AAA-rated. | Cloud price war with AWS |
| 2 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | Search is a near-monopoly, and YouTube, Cloud and Waymo are growth options. Excluding its large cash pile, it trades around 20x earnings. | Antitrust, EU fines |
| 3 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | It's about 25% below its September high. AWS is growing about 45% with high margins, and advertising is a new profit engine. | Regulation, heavy spending |
| 4 | **Visa (V)** | It collects a toll on the global shift from cash to cards. It has very high margins and doesn't take credit risk. | Fintech disruption, fee regulation |
| 5 | **UnitedHealth (UNH)** | It's the largest managed-care company, and its Optum health-services unit is growing fast. "Medicare for All" headlines have hurt the stock more than the fundamentals. | Healthcare policy in the 2020 election |
| 6 | **Adobe (ADBE)** | Its creative and document software has moved to subscriptions, and the Magento and Marketo deals build out its marketing software. Revenue is growing more than 20%. | Rich valuation |
| 7 | **ASML (ASML)** | It is the only maker of EUV lithography machines, which start high-volume production in 2019. Every leading-edge chip will need its tools. | Chip-cycle swings, export controls |
| 8 | **TSMC (TSM)** | It leads in 7nm chip manufacturing while Intel's 10nm process is years late. Apple, AMD and Huawei depend on it. | China/Taiwan tension, customer concentration |
| 9 | **NVIDIA (NVDA)** | It's down about 50% since October because of excess crypto-related inventory. That looks temporary, while its data-center AI business is structural. *(This is the most hindsight-tainted pick; it was a contested call in 2019.)* | Inventory clearing could take longer, competition |
| 10 | **Costco (COST)** | This is the defensive holding. Membership fees provide steady income, renewal rates are about 90%, and it holds up well in recessions. | Valuation, thin margins |

**Alternates:** Facebook (a contrarian bet at about 17x earnings after its privacy scandals), Thermo Fisher, Intuitive Surgical and Mastercard.

## How to hold it

- **Watch the tech concentration.** Half the list is tech or semiconductors, and three picks (ASML, TSMC, NVIDIA) are exposed to the trade war. Apple's revenue warning, issued after the close today, shows that China risk is real.
- **Size the positions.** Equal weights of 10% each, rebalanced once a year, keep one mistake from sinking the portfolio.
- **Stagger your purchases.** Volatility is high, so buying in 3–4 tranches over a few months reduces timing risk.
- **Consider a core-and-satellite setup.** A 10-stock portfolio is concentrated. Keeping an S&P index fund as the core and using these picks as satellites lowers the chance of badly lagging the market.
- **Remember the base rate.** Most professional managers fail to beat the S&P 500 over five years, and the index is a tough benchmark to beat.

*This is not personalized financial advice.*

If you'd like, I can step out of 2019 and score this list against the S&P 500's actual total return from January 2019 to January 2024. That would show how much of the result came from the reasoning and how much from luck or hindsight.
